rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~83% (from ~77%); BoE Nov 5 hike to 4.00% ~97%; ECB Dec ~89%; BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~56%; RBNZ Dec ~57%; RBA easing priced by end-2027
rows.read: Most big central banks still lean toward higher rates, and the Bank of England is set to raise on Thursday. Bets on a December Fed hike rose even as the dollar fell, so US rate support is intact. Currencies are moving on hints about the next step, not on hikes already expected.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US ADP +86K (fcst +67K); ISM services 54.5 (fcst 54.8); Canada goods trade surplus C$5.35B Sep (fcst ~C$4.1B); China services PMI 50.8 (from 51.6)
rows.read: US figures were mixed: hiring at private firms beat forecasts while the services survey slipped a little but stayed healthy. A Democratic Congress is expected to spend less, which could slow US growth next year. Canada's trade surplus beat, though its exports are still shrinking.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Euro-area flash CPI 4.0% Oct (fcst 4.0%, core 2.5%); ISM services prices paid ~73; Brent $94.29 (−9%); Swiss CPI 1.5% Oct
rows.read: Euro-area inflation rose as expected, driven by energy, which keeps a December rate hike there on track without adding urgency. Oil's sharp fall, if it lasts, would ease price pressure almost everywhere and take some heat off central banks. For now, US service firms still report high costs.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: Nikkei ~−3% (Asia); S&P 500 ~+1.8% by midday; USD/JPY 158.29; USD/CHF 0.8162; AUD/USD 0.7008; gold ~$4,059
rows.read: Asia sold off on the US midterm results, but Wall Street rallied hard, reading a split government and a possible end to the Iran war as calmer, not riskier. Safe havens like the franc and yen gave back early gains, and growth-linked currencies like the Aussie recovered. Gold rose anyway, helped by the weaker dollar.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent $94.29 (−8.9%, lowest since Sep 4); WTI $87.70 (−8.7%); EIA crude stocks −0.9M bbl (fcst −1.7M)
rows.read: Oil fell about 9% in a day on bets the Iran war winds down. That cuts the energy bill for importers like Japan and the euro area and trims income for exporters like Canada. The loonie held up only because the US dollar fell faster.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Oct 27: funds strongly against CAD, against EUR (real money for), against NZD, for AUD (real money strongly against), strongly for gold (cut); oil net long among weakest since 2015
rows.read: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and they are also betting against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Their large bets on gold have been shrinking. New figures arrive Friday.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: AP calls the House for Democrats (Senate called Nov 3); Treasury refunding $125B, unchanged; Canada budget Nov 5, 3:00 PM CT; Fitch France A+ negative (Oct 30)
rows.read: Democrats now control both houses of Congress, so President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which takes some support away from the dollar. The US Treasury kept its bond sales unchanged, adding no new pressure on yields. Canada presents its federal budget on Thursday, and France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.
